feedback: If a learner says a sealed 'empty' bottle contains nothing, have them squeeze it and feel the trapped air push back.

If a learner says gas weighs nothing, note the invisibility is why it feels that way; weighing a ball pumped up hard and then the same ball when soft, on a sensitive balance, can provide counter-evidence (a balloon blown up by mouth usually shows no measurable difference).
activities.intendedInsight: Gases are real matter: they take up space and have mass, even though they are usually invisible. An 'empty' sealed bottle is actually full of air.
learnerActions: Trap air by sealing a bag or squeezing a capped bottle; feel the resistance and note the gas takes up space.
Blow bubbles or feel a puff of air on your hand to sense that the invisible gas is really there.

Compare a ball pumped up hard (e.g. a football inflated with a pump) with the same ball when soft. If a sensitive balance is available, weigh it both ways: the hard-pumped ball should weigh slightly more because extra air has been squeezed in. Discuss whether the gas has mass. (A balloon blown up by mouth is not a good test: the air inside is barely squeezed, so a classroom balance will show little or no difference.)
Answer: can you see the air in this room? Is it still a gas even though it's invisible?
activities.title: Gas is real stuff

feedback: If a learner is stuck on honey because it is 'in between', ask whether it keeps its own shape or slowly takes the jar's shape and forms a level surface over time (liquid behaviour).
If a learner classifies foam by how light it feels, redirect to the behaviour test: does it keep its own shape?
A recognition-only sort can show the final answer; ask the learner to state the behavioural evidence as well, so you can check the reasoning and not just the conclusion.
activities.intendedInsight: Consistent behaviour-based criteria help classify awkward materials: very thick liquids (honey) and very light solids (solid foams such as a sponge or polystyrene) are judged by whether they keep their own shape, take a container's shape, or fill the space. Some materials, such as shaving foam, toothpaste or jelly, are mixtures that show some solid-like and some liquid-like behaviour, so it is fine to say they do not fit neatly.
learnerActions: Sort at least eight everyday materials into solid, liquid or gas, writing the behaviour reason for each.

Include genuinely tricky items — honey, jelly/gel, toothpaste, a solid foam such as a sponge — and decide each by behaviour rather than by how thick or light it feels; if an item shows both solid-like and liquid-like behaviour (e.g. toothpaste or shaving foam), record that it is a tricky mixture and describe what it does.
For each item answer 'which behaviour proves it?' by matching it to one of the three tests.
Explain aloud why sand is a solid and why the kettle cloud is not the gas.
activities.title: Classify and check: the eight-plus material sort
